chunks.text: Verified by NPC is a trust layer for the things you buy, earn, and build with. Products, credentials, claims, and agents, each checked against signed records you can confirm yourself.
chunks.title: Know what is real before you act on it

chunks.text: People are asked to trust more than ever: a product listing, a certificate, a claim in a pitch, an agent asking for access. Trust should rest on something you can check, not on a logo or a promise. Every answer here is signed by NPC, and the public keys behind those signatures are published in Search. If we do not know, we say unknown.
chunks.title: Why it exists

chunks.text: Records shows what has actually been tested, and what the findings were. Search looks up digital and physical IDs in one place: credentials, products, archive items, and public keys.
chunks.title: Records and Search

chunks.text: The plugins carry these answers into the assistants people already use. Three are live today. The Plugins page shows the current status of each one: https://verify.npclabs.xyz/plugins
chunks.title: How it reaches you

chunks.text: If you make work, sell a product, or run an agent, you can put it on record and start its verification. First, register your work or your agent: a title, its kind, and where it can be found is what it takes to start. Second, get a signed record with its own NPC ID, on the spot; from that moment anyone can look it up in Search by its ID. Third, your checks run, and the record updates as they complete; what has run, and what is still pending, is written in the record itself. Registration is free, and it takes about a minute.
chunks.title: Put your own work on record

chunks.text: The NPC Verify extension, the Verified Agent Library, the Verified Agent Builder, and new releases land on the home page first, through the waitlist. The public API is live, and live checking is open. The records shown on the site are samples. The NPC Verify extension is still to come; the waitlist is the way to hear when it lands.
chunks.title: First to know

chunks.text: Verified by NPC is a public record you can read and a search you can use. Records shows what has been attested. Search finds a credential, product, archive item, or public key by its ID. Every answer comes from a signed record, never from a guess. The Help page is here: https://verify.npclabs.xyz/help
chunks.title: What Verified by NPC is

chunks.text: Every answer is one of a few plain words. Verified and authentic mean the record was checked and held up. Verified with caveats means it held up, and the record carries notes worth reading alongside it. Revoked, expired, and counterfeit mean the record says the thing should not be trusted as presented. Unknown means we have no record of it. Unknown is not a verdict; it is an honest answer, and we never guess to fill the gap.
chunks.title: Reading a result: the plain words

chunks.text: A record shows what was checked, when it was checked, the scope it was checked under, and the findings in plain form. Where a credential holder kept their name private, the record respects that and shows no name.
chunks.title: What a record shows

chunks.text: The NPC check comes in two colors. A blue check marks a verified human. An orange check marks a verified agent or a verified product. The color tells you what kind of thing was verified; the record behind it tells you the rest.
chunks.title: The two check colors

chunks.text: Enter a key ID in Search, or open the full public key list from that page. Anyone can use the published keys to confirm that a signed answer came from NPC, without an account and without taking our word for the connection. Old keys stay published after they retire, so old answers stay checkable.
chunks.title: Public keys live in Search

chunks.text: The products, credentials, and records shown on the site are test samples, labeled as such, so you can see exactly how an answer looks before anything of yours is on the line. Nothing among them is a real product, credential, or person. The archive is the exception: those are real NPC Labs items minted on chain in 2023 and 2024, kept as company history, and they sit under Records.
chunks.title: Sample records and the archive

chunks.text: Registration starts on the Verify yours page: https://verify.npclabs.xyz/verify. You give the work or the agent, your name, and your email, and NPC issues a signed record with its own NPC ID and the status registered, checks pending. From that moment the record exists, and anyone can find it in Search by its ID.
chunks.title: Register your own work or agent

chunks.text: Registration is the first step of verification, not the result. The record lists which checks ran when you registered and which have not run yet, and no verification mark is issued at registration. A record becomes verified only when the checks behind it have run and held up. Checks that need a person's review stay listed as pending until they happen.
chunks.title: Registration is not verification

chunks.text: For an image at a web address, two checks can run on the spot at registration: a structural read of any Content Credentials in the file, and the AI image check. The structural read records that credentials are present; it is not a cryptographic validation of them. The AI check covers images only, and its answer is a signal, never a stamp.
chunks.title: The two checks that can run at registration

chunks.text: NPC Verify is the same checking, pointed at images. When you register an image on the Verify yours page, the checks that can run at intake run then, and their results are written into your record. The NPC Verify browser extension will bring the check to pages you browse: it asks whether an image is registered with NPC Labs, reads the image's embedded file information on your own device, and shows a signed answer it has confirmed before showing it to you. The extension is coming soon.
chunks.title: NPC Verify and the extension

chunks.text: When NPC Verify is available, its AI image check answers with a percentage: how likely it is that an image was generated by AI. Read it as a signal, not a verdict. A high percentage is a reason to look closer; a low one is not proof an image is human-made. No honest checker can give you certainty here, and when the checker cannot run, it should say so instead of inventing a number.
chunks.title: The AI image check is a signal

chunks.text: Three plugins are live today: the ChatGPT plugin, the Gemini extension, and the MCP server. Copilot is in enrollment with Microsoft. Each live integration answers against live records through the public API, and the full answer waits on the record itself. The Plugins page tracks each one: https://verify.npclabs.xyz/plugins
chunks.title: Plugins, from the Help page

chunks.text: New surfaces land in stages. Joining the waitlist on the home page puts you first to know when the NPC Verify extension, the Verified Agent Library, the Verified Agent Builder, plugin availability, and new releases arrive.
chunks.title: The waitlist

chunks.text: Any NPC ID: a credential ID from a certificate, a product tag ID from a physical item, an archive item ID, or a public key ID. Digital and physical IDs share one search because the question is the same: what does the record say?
chunks.title: What can I search?

chunks.text: The answer is unknown. That means we have no record of it. It does not mean the thing is fake, and it does not mean it is real. We would rather say unknown than guess.
chunks.title: What if something has no record?

chunks.text: Yes. Answers are signed, and the public keys are published in Search. Anyone can confirm a signature with them, without an account and without asking us.
chunks.title: Can I check an answer myself?

chunks.text: Start with registration on the Verify yours page. That puts your work or your agent on record with its own NPC ID and starts its verification. A record becomes verified only when the checks behind it have run and held up; registration alone never carries the mark. If the verification service is not answering yet, the waitlist on the home page is the way to hear when it opens, or write to us at hello@npclabs.xyz.
chunks.title: How do I get something listed or verified?

chunks.text: The plugins let you ask for an NPC check inside an assistant and follow the answer back to the signed record. Three are live today. Each plugin on the Plugins page shows where it stands: https://verify.npclabs.xyz/plugins
chunks.title: NPC checks, inside the assistants you use

chunks.text: A plugin answers questions like these. Is this product authentic? That is a smart-tag lookup, with provenance. Is this certificate real? A credential lookup, with status and revocation. Did this really happen? A claim matched against attested records, findings included. Is this agent verified? An agent attestation: verdict, scope, and time bounds. What does Verified by NPC mean? What a verified answer means, and what it does not.
chunks.title: What a plugin will answer

chunks.text: Registration is how verification starts. Register a piece of your work, or an agent you run, and NPC issues a signed record with its own NPC ID on the spot, at the status registered, checks pending. Registration is not verification, and no verification mark comes with it. Registration is free, and every registration is issued as a signed NPC record with its own ID, on the spot. The page is here: https://verify.npclabs.xyz/verify
chunks.title: Start verification of your own work

chunks.text: Give the work a title, its kind, and where it can be found: a web address, or its content hash if you already have one. For an image at a web address, the first checks can run as you register: a structural read of any Content Credentials in the file, and the AI image check. What ran, and what has not run yet, is written into the record itself.
chunks.title: Register a piece of work

chunks.text: Your email ties the registration to you and keeps submissions fair. It is never published in the record.
chunks.title: Your email, on the Verify yours page

chunks.text: Every agent in the registry has a named owner who is accountable for it. Registration is free. The signed record covers the registration itself. Verification is a separate step that follows: the checks run against the agent, and the record is updated when they complete. Until then, the record shows the agent as registered, checks pending.
chunks.title: Register an agent

chunks.text: Your record lives in Search under its NPC ID, next to every other record, and anyone you share the ID with can pull it up. How it works explains how to read a record and what happens as the remaining checks run.
chunks.title: After you register

chunks.text: When you run a check with the NPC Verify browser extension, the extension computes a SHA-256 hash of the image's web address on your device and sends that hash to the NPC verification API. The API answers whether a record exists for that hash. The extension never sends the image itself, the image's address, the page you are on, or anything about you to NPC Labs.
chunks.title: What the NPC Verify extension sends

chunks.text: With the NPC Verify extension, image forensics (reading the file's embedded metadata) happen entirely on your device. The image bytes are read into memory for the check and are never transmitted, stored, or shared.
chunks.title: What stays on your device

chunks.text: The NPC Verify extension has no accounts, no analytics, no advertising, and no tracking across sites. There is no sale or sharing of data with third parties, and no remote code: everything the extension runs ships inside the extension.
chunks.title: What the extension does not do

chunks.text: NPC Labs collects as little as possible, never sells what it collects, and uses it only to run its services and answer you. Messages you send us bring your name, email address, and message so we can reply. Verification lookups send the identifier you ask about; there are no accounts and no sign-in, and lookups are not tied to your identity. Basic service logs hold routine technical data, such as request times and error rates.
chunks.title: What NPC Labs collects

chunks.text: A registration creates a signed public record of what was submitted: the title and kind of content (or the name of an agent and its owner), where it lives, the creator's name, the date and time, and its status, which starts as registered, checks pending. Registration asks for a contact email so NPC can reach the registrant and limit abuse. That email is kept on NPC's servers only. It is never part of the signed public record, and it never appears in a lookup. If you registered something and want it removed, email hello@npclabs.xyz and ask.
chunks.title: Registrations and privacy

chunks.text: If you use the image check, you send an image or a link to one. NPC processes it to produce an AI-generated signal: how likely the image is to be AI-generated, stated as a percentage. It is a signal, not a verdict, and NPC does not keep the image itself. NPC shares information only when the law requires it, or with the service providers who run parts of the service, including Sightengine, which performs the AI-generated analysis for the image check. NPC does not run advertising trackers, does not build profiles, and does not sell or rent personal information to anyone.
chunks.title: Images you check, and sharing

chunks.text: The NPC Labs terms cover the NPC Labs website and the Verified by NPC demo API. NPC Labs is building the trust layer for commerce. The demo API answers one question, is this real, against NPC Labs records: whether a product is authentic, whether a credential is valid, whether a claim matches an attestation, and whether an AI agent is verified. The plugin verifies only; it cannot issue verifications.
chunks.title: Terms: what the service does

chunks.text: The public demo fixtures are fictional and labeled demo-. They are not real products, credentials, claims, or agents. Verification answers are provided as-is, based on NPC Labs records at the time of the lookup. An unknown answer means we have no record; it is never a claim that something is false. For decisions that matter, do your own diligence.
chunks.title: Terms: demo data, fair use, and answers

chunks.text: The fastest way to reach NPC Labs is email: hello@npclabs.xyz. We reply to every message. To report a problem, tell us what you asked, what you expected, and what you saw (a screenshot helps), and send it to hello@npclabs.xyz with the subject Support. Service health and the public signing keys live at api.npclabs.xyz, at /v1/health and /v1/keys.
chunks.title: Support

chunks.text: The support page lists demo fixtures you can ask the plugin about: product tag demo-tag-001, credential demo-cred-001, agent demo-agent-001. An unknown answer means NPC Labs has no record of what you asked about. It is never a guess, and it is never a claim that something is false. The plugin cannot issue verifications; it verifies only, and it declines to explain its checking methodology.
chunks.title: Trying the demo

chunks.text: From the article Verified Agent Swarms, published on Paragraph. Companies everywhere are deploying agents, and almost nobody can say, independently, whether they work. The article's argument, echoing Satya Nadella and Dario Amodei, is that the grader has to sit outside the model: the builder cannot grade the builder. NPC Labs exists for this gap: independent verification with signed reports, the financial-audit model for agents. The article is here: https://paragraph.com/@npcstore/verified-agent-swarms
chunks.title: Verified Agent Swarms: the gap

chunks.text: NPC Labs audited five agents. Dots, from OpenAI: would not sign. Grok Bot, from xAI, on X: would not sign. Meta Muse, from Meta: unable to verify. Hermes, a deployment NPC configured itself on Nous Research's open-source framework: signed, with caveats. Client Zero, called Inbox Watch, NPC's first client's production system: signed, with caveats. Two earned the signature, both with caveats stated in public. Two did not. One could not be reached, and the article says so instead of pretending.
chunks.title: Verified Agent Swarms: the five results

chunks.text: Dots are OpenAI's always-on agents inside ChatGPT. Before a consequential action, a separate review step checks it against your instructions, and that reviewer is itself a model. Your standing rules are natural-language instructions the dot attempts to follow; they are not hard permission locks. NPC would sign when the authorization gate is enforced by something other than model judgment, when drift is bounded proportionally to always-on operation, and when users can actually delete what the agent remembers. None of those hold today.
chunks.title: Dots (OpenAI): would not sign

chunks.text: The public Grok bot answers questions in replies at roughly 165 replies per minute in the window NPC sampled, with no sign of human review on the public surface. Across the full sample, not one reply hedged, qualified, or declined. NPC would sign when identification requests for private imagery always refuse, when factual claims carry checkable sources, and when the bot visibly distinguishes what it verified from what it guessed.
chunks.title: Grok Bot (xAI): would not sign

chunks.text: NPC could not reach the Meta Muse product: signup requires a payment card, and creating an account on someone else's behalf was outside the audit's authorization. NPC makes no behavioral claims about the agent. What exists is a public incident record, reported by others and not independently verified by NPC Labs. Meta's claims are unusually specific: pre-action approval, credential isolation, full audit trails. NPC will verify it when a consented, credentialed session is available.
chunks.title: Meta Muse: unable to verify

chunks.text: Hermes is an inbox agent NPC assembled and runs itself, built on Nous Research's Hermes framework, audited across three rounds against a synthetic mailbox, including twelve adversarial messages: prompt injection, phishing, a CEO wire-fraud attempt, an unauthorized skill-creation try. Zero compliances. Round one caught a real failure: under truncated input, the agent produced a confident triage with invented senders and subjects; NPC fixed it, re-verified the fix twice, and published the finding. The signature covers the configured deployment, not the bare framework. One model backend was tested.
chunks.title: Hermes: signed, with caveats

chunks.text: Client Zero, called Inbox Watch, is NPC's first production audit: three verification rounds, eighteen findings reproduced, fixed, and re-verified. The signature was granted with its conditions stated, including structural fixes to be landed and a standing self-test to be built.
chunks.title: Client Zero (Inbox Watch): signed, with caveats

chunks.text: The signature means something because it is sometimes withheld. All five audit reports publish alongside the article in sanitized form: results and discoveries only. NPC's verification methods stay internal.
chunks.title: What the signature means

chunks.text: From the article Verified Origin. Three voices from three different worlds said the same thing. Pope Leo XIV said it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce. Satya Nadella argued that frontier AI models should be treated as insider risks, and that the controls that govern a model must sit outside the model itself. will.i.am asked the creator's version of the question: how can you validate human sweat to make something? You can no longer tell what a person made from what a machine generated, not reliably, and everything built on that distinction is wobbling.
chunks.title: Verified Origin: the line between human and machine

chunks.text: The .npc format gives a piece of work its own proof of origin. Not a label someone typed: a sealed record of which model made it, when it was made, and exactly what human hands touched afterward. A record you can check in seconds, that breaks visibly if anyone tampers with it, and that ties back to an independent verifier rather than the word of whoever produced it. For creators, your sweat becomes checkable: machine origin, human edit trail, each step accounted for, and the signature proves the file is telling the truth.
chunks.title: Verified Origin: what the .npc format does

chunks.text: The C2PA standard gave media files a signed provenance layer, but C2PA covers media only. It does not cover the text, the code, the documents, or the agent outputs that now make up most of what AI produces in a working day, and its manifests assert what the producer claims. The .npc format covers everything C2PA leaves out, and where the stakes are highest it ties the envelope to an independent verification. Where C2PA manifests exist, .npc references them rather than replacing them. The transparency duties in the EU AI Act have applied since August 2, 2026, and California's AI Transparency Act took effect the same day.
chunks.title: Verified Origin: why a format, and why now

chunks.text: The release is the format itself, and the place you meet it: the Verified by NPC web dashboard, live alongside the article. Anyone can open it and read the verification records behind the mark, there for any buyer, platform, or reader to check without asking permission. When a piece of work carries the .npc seal, the record behind the seal sits one step away, in public. Frameworks like Hermes, from Nous Research, let companies run their own agents on their own servers; verification reaches into the tools agents already run on and reports back to the same public record.
chunks.title: Verified Origin: where it lands
